concepts.title: CLIP Training Procedure

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP is trained by maximizing the dot product between matched image-text pairs and minimizing it for mismatched pairs within a batch.
concepts.content:
CLIP training begins by sampling a batch of $N$ language-image pairs, ${\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}}_{i=1}^N$. These text strings and images are embedded using a language encoder $f_t$ and an image encoder $f_\ell$, respectively, producing a set of text embeddings ${\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_t}_{i=1}^N$ and image embeddings ${\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell}_{i=1}^N$. To compute the loss, the dot product $\mathbf{z}^{(i)}_\ell\cdot \mathbf{z}^{(j)}_t$ is calculated for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,N\}$. Terms where $i == j$ represent positive pairs, and the objective is to maximize these dot products. Terms where $i \neq j$ are negative pairs, and the objective is to minimize these dot products.

(see figure: CLIP training for one batch of six language-image training examples. Green boxes are positive pairings (we seek to increase their value); these are the six training pairs. Red boxes are negative...)
concepts.motivation_md: CLIP aims to learn a robust representation of visual concepts by leveraging the rich semantic information available in natural language descriptions, rather than relying on fixed categorical labels.
concepts.recap_md: - Sample a batch of $N$ image-text pairs and embed them into a shared vector space.

slots.motivation: CLIP aims to learn a robust representation of visual concepts by leveraging the rich semantic information available in natural language descriptions, rather than relying on fixed categorical labels.

concepts.title: Visualizing CLIP Embeddings with t-SNE

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: t-SNE visualization of CLIP encoders reveals that image layers transition from grouping by color to shape, while text encoders treat both features with similar ease.
concepts.content:
A trained CLIP model maps data to embeddings in a way that can be visualized using t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) for each encoder. For the image encoder, early layers tend to group images by color, while later layers group them more by shape. In contrast, for the text encoder, color words and shape words are equally easy to group. This difference may arise because color is a superficial feature in pixel-space whereas shape requires more processing to extract; however, in text-space, both concepts are represented by words that are equally accessible to the model.

(see figure: CLIP @radford2021learning mapping diagram, using the same technique as described in @sec-neural_nets_as_distribution_transformers. To reduce dimensionality we apply t-SNE @tsne separately for the...)
concepts.motivation_md: Visualizing the internal representations of CLIP helps researchers understand how different modalities (images vs. text) process features like color and shape at various stages of the network.
concepts.recap_md: - Use t-SNE to reduce the dimensionality of image and text embeddings for visualization.

concepts.title: CLIP Shared Embedding Space

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP aligns normalized image and text embeddings on a hypersphere, placing matching descriptions and images in close proximity.
concepts.content:
After passing data through the encoders, the final stage is to normalize the outputs and compute the alignment between the image and text embeddings. Once normalized, all embeddings lie on the surface of a hypersphere. In this shared space, text descriptions are embedded near the image embeddings that match those descriptions. Visualizing this $768$-dimensional space in 2D can be achieved using kernel principle component analysis with a cosine kernel, often removing the first principle component to account for the global offset between image and text modalities.

(see figure: CLIP @radford2021learning joint embedding)
concepts.motivation_md: Normalizing embeddings to a hypersphere allows the model to use cosine similarity as a consistent metric for comparing how well a text description matches an image.
concepts.recap_md: - Normalize embeddings so they lie on a hypersphere for alignment.

concepts.title: Kernel Principle Component Analysis

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Kernel Principle Component Analysis is a technique used to visualize high-dimensional embeddings by applying a kernel to capture non-linear relationships.
concepts.content: Kernel principle component analysis is applied to embeddings, often using a cosine kernel. In the context of CLIP, the first principle component is sometimes removed because it codes for a global offset between the image embeddings and text embeddings, allowing for a clearer visualization of the alignment between the two modalities.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard PCA only captures linear relationships; Kernel PCA allows for the dimensionality reduction of data that lies on non-linear manifolds, such as embeddings on a hypersphere.

concepts.title: Zero-Shot Classification with CLIP

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP enables zero-shot classification by leveraging the compositional power of language to describe and identify novel image categories without specific training.
concepts.content: Using language as one of the views in contrastive methods allows CLIP to connect the domain of images to the domain of language. This connection makes the powerful compositional abilities of language applicable to imagery. For example, CLIP can create a novel image classifier on the fly by describing a category in English, such as "striped red circles" versus "polka dotted green squares." CLIP leverages the ability of language to compose concepts to construct an image classifier for these categories without requiring explicit training on those specific labels.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional classifiers are limited to a fixed set of labels; zero-shot classification allows models to generalize to any concept that can be described in text.
concepts.recap_md: - Use natural language to define new conceptual categories on the fly.

concepts.title: CLIP Inference Procedure

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP performs inference by comparing the embedding of a query image to the embeddings of several candidate text descriptions to find the best match.
concepts.content:
To classify an image using CLIP, given a set of sentences ${\mathbf{t}^{a}, \mathbf{t}^{b}, \ldots}$ describing classes $a, b$, etc.:

1. Embed each sentence into a $\mathbf{z}$-vector: $\mathbf{z}_t^{a} = f_t(\mathbf{t}^{a}), \mathbf{z}_t^{b} = f_t(\mathbf{t}^{b})$, and so on.
2. Embed the query image into a $\mathbf{z}$-vector: $\mathbf{z}_{\ell}^{q} = f_{\ell}(\boldsymbol\ell^{q})$.
3. Determine which sentence embedding is closest to the image embedding; that is the predicted class.

(see figure: Making a ``striped red circles'' (class $a$) versus ``polka dotted green square'' (class $b$) classifier using a trained CLIP. The CLIP model parameters are frozen and not updated. Instead the...)
concepts.motivation_md: This procedure allows for flexible, open-vocabulary image classification where the model does not need to be retrained to recognize new classes.
concepts.recap_md: - Embed candidate text descriptions and the query image into the same space.

concepts.title: Custom Classifiers with CLIP

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Custom classifiers can be built in CLIP by comparing the angular distance between an image embedding and multiple text-based class vectors.
concepts.content:
Custom binary or multi-class classifiers can be created by describing classes with text strings (e.g., "triangle" versus "circle"). The embeddings of these text descriptions serve as class vectors. To classify an image, the system checks whether the image embedding is closer in angular distance to one text vector or another. This approach is extensible; adding more text vectors allows the space to be partitioned in more ways to accommodate additional classes.

[FIGURE:bbc557ba56150a05 | A scatter plot showing data points arranged in a circular pattern on a 2D coordinate system ranging from -1.0 to 1.0 on both axes. The points are represented by different shapes (triangles, squares...]
concepts.motivation_md: This enables users to build specialized classifiers for niche tasks instantly, without collecting or labeling a training dataset.
concepts.recap_md: - Define classes using text strings and convert them to embeddings.

concepts.title: Translating between Images and Text
concepts.one_liner: X2Y systems use deep networks to translate between disparate data modalities, such as images to text or music to lyrics.
concepts.content: It is possible to translate between entirely different data modalities using deep networks. For any data type X and any other type Y, "X2Y" (and "Y2X") systems can forge links between disparate domains of knowledge. Examples include translating between images and sounds, music and lyrics, or amino acid sequences and protein geometry. These systems are powerful because they allow tools and discoveries from one domain to become applicable to other linked domains.
concepts.motivation_md: Cross-modal translation allows for the integration of knowledge across different formats, enabling tasks like image captioning, text-to-image generation, and cross-domain search.
concepts.recap_md: - Use deep networks to map one data modality (X) to another (Y).

concepts.title: Word-level Encoding
concepts.one_liner: Word-level encoding represents text by mapping each unique word in a vocabulary to a specific one-hot code.
concepts.content: One option for representing text as numbers is to use a word-level encoding scheme. This involves mapping each word in a vocabulary to a unique one-hot code. For a vocabulary containing $K$ different words, this requires $K$-dimensional one-hot codes.
concepts.motivation_md: To process text with neural networks, words must be converted into a numerical format that the model can interpret.

  "- The dimensionality of the vector is equal to the size of the vocabulary $K$." 
]

concepts.title: Character-level Encoding
concepts.one_liner: Character-level encoding assigns a one-hot code to each individual character rather than to entire words.
concepts.content: Character-level encoding is a strategy where a one-hot code is assigned to each character in the vocabulary rather than to each unique word. If all alphanumeric characters and common punctuation marks are represented this way, it may only require a few dozen codes. However, the disadvantage is that representing a single word now requires a sequence of one-hots, which necessitates modeling that sequence.
concepts.motivation_md: Character-level encoding significantly reduces the vocabulary size compared to word-level encoding and can handle out-of-vocabulary words more gracefully.

concepts.title: Modular Encoder-Decoder Translation
concepts.one_liner: One approach to solving X-to-Y translation problems is to hook up an encoder for domain X to a decoder for domain Y.
concepts.content: One approach to solving X-to-Y translation problems is to do it in a modular fashion by hooking up an encoder for domain X to a decoder for domain Y. This approach is popular because powerful encoder and decoder architectures, as well as pretrained models, exist for many domains. If we have an encoder $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$ and a decoder $g: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$, then we can create a translator simply by function composition, $g \circ f$.
concepts.motivation_md: Translation between different modalities (like text and images) is complex. By using a modular approach, researchers can leverage specialized, pre-existing models for each domain and combine them into a single system, rather than training a massive end-to-end model from scratch for every specific pair of domains.
concepts.recap_md: - Translation can be achieved by composing an encoder $f$ and a decoder $g$ into a single function $g \circ f$.

concepts.title: Encoder-Decoder Alignment Strategies
concepts.one_liner: Alignment strategies ensure that the output of an encoder is interpretable as a proper input to a specific decoder.
concepts.content:
The output of an encoder might not be interpretable as a proper input to the selected decoder. For example, if $f$ is a text encoder and $g$ is an image decoder, the generated image $\boldsymbol\ell= g(f(\mathbf{t}))$ from text input $\mathbf{t}$ is not guaranteed to semantically match the text.

To align the encoder and decoder, several strategies can be followed. One is to finetune the composition $g \circ f$ on paired examples of the target translation problem, $\{\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$. Another option is to freeze $f$ and $g$ and instead train a translation function in latent space, $h: \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow \mathcal{Z}$, so that $g \circ h \circ f$ correctly maps each training point $\mathbf{t}^{(i)}$ to the target output $\boldsymbol\ell^{(i)}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Even if we have a good encoder and a good decoder, their latent spaces may not naturally match. Alignment strategies are necessary to bridge the gap between these representations so that the decoder correctly interprets the information provided by the encoder.
concepts.recap_md: - Alignment can be achieved by finetuning the entire composed model on paired data.

concepts.title: Text-to-Image Synthesis
concepts.one_liner: Text-to-image synthesis is the process of generating an image from a text description using conditional generative models.
concepts.content:
One amazing ability of modern generative models is to synthesize an image just from a text description, a problem called text-to-image. This can be achieved using conditional generative models by finding an effective way to use text as the conditioning information. (see figure: Text-to-image.)

This mapping from the space of text to the space of images allows a system to translate input text $\mathbf{t}$ to an output image $\hat{\boldsymbol\ell}$ that matches what the text describes. This problem is closely related to concepts in representation learning and generative modeling.
concepts.motivation_md: Text-to-image synthesis allows for the creation of visual content through natural language, making generative AI accessible for creative tasks, design, and visual communication.
concepts.recap_md: - Text-to-image synthesis maps text descriptions to corresponding visual representations.

concepts.title: Text-to-Image with Conditional Variational Autoencoders
concepts.one_liner: A conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) for text-to-image uses a text encoder to provide conditioning vectors for image generation.
concepts.content:
A conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) can be used for text-to-image synthesis, an architecture notably used by the DALL-E 1 model. A cVAE for text-to-image is trained like a regular cVAE, but specifically uses a text encoder—a neural network that maps text to a vector embedding.

(see figure: Training a cVAE to perform text-to-image. The dotted lines indicate that the image encoder is only used during training; at test time, usage follows the solid path. In this cartoon we draw the output...)

After training, we can sample from the model by discarding the image encoder. Instead, we input a random Gaussian vector to the decoder and provide the decoder with the text embedding to generate the image.

(see figure: Sampling from a trained cVAE.)
concepts.motivation_md: The cVAE framework provides a structured way to learn a latent space that is conditioned on text, allowing for diverse image generation from the same prompt by sampling from a distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Text-to-image cVAEs use a text encoder to condition the image generation process.

concepts.title: Text-to-Image with Conditional Diffusion Models
concepts.one_liner: Conditional diffusion models generate images from text by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise conditioned on text embeddings.
concepts.content:
Text-to-image generation can also be performed using a conditional diffusion model, an approach used by DALL-E 2 and other popular systems. A key challenge is effectively inserting text embeddings into the decoder. One method is to insert text embedding vectors into each denoising U-Net, and even into multiple layers of each U-Net, allowing the model to condition all decisions on the text information.

(see figure: A text-to-image diffusion model.)

At sampling time, both conditional diffusion models and cVAEs take text and Gaussian noise as input. While a VAE uses a network that maps these inputs to an image in a single forward pass, a diffusion model maps to an image via a chain of denoising steps, each being a forward pass through a neural network.
concepts.motivation_md: Diffusion models often produce higher-quality and more detailed images than VAEs. By conditioning the iterative denoising process on text, the model can refine the image to better match the description at multiple scales.
concepts.recap_md: - Diffusion models generate images through iterative denoising steps rather than a single forward pass.

concepts.title: Image-to-Text (Image Captioning)
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-text, or image captioning, translates visual information into natural language descriptions.
concepts.content:
Naturally, we can also translate in the opposite direction using an image encoder and a text decoder. This problem is called image-to-text or image captioning. This translation is useful because language serves as a general-purpose interface for human knowledge; translating images to text links imagery to many other domains.

concepts.title: Cross-Attention Layer
concepts.one_liner: The cross-attention layer allows text tokens to attend to image tokens, integrating visual information into a text decoder.
concepts.content: The cross-attention layer (`cross-attn`) addresses the question of how to insert image tokens into a text model. In this layer, text tokens attend to image tokens. The image tokens emit their value vectors, which are mixed with the text token value vectors according to the attention weights to produce the next layer of tokens in the text decoder.
concepts.motivation_md: In multimodal tasks, the model needs a way to relate information from one modality (like an image) to another (like text). Cross-attention provides a mechanism for the text generation process to 'look at' specific parts of the image representation.
concepts.recap_md: - Cross-attention enables interaction between different modalities by letting one set of tokens attend to another.

slots.motivation: In multimodal tasks, the model needs a way to relate information from one modality (like an image) to another (like text). Cross-attention provides a mechanism for the text generation process to 'look at' specific parts of the image representation.

concepts.title: Cross-Attention Equations
concepts.one_liner: Cross-attention equations define how queries from text tokens interact with keys and values from image tokens.
concepts.motivation_md: Formalizing cross-attention with equations allows for the precise implementation of multimodal transformers, where text and image features must be mathematically combined through a shared attention mechanism.
concepts.recap_md: - Cross-attention uses text-based queries $\mathbf{Q}_t$ and image-based keys $\mathbf{K}_\ell$ and values $\mathbf{V}_\ell$.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Text Decoding for Image Captioning
concepts.one_liner: An autoregressive text decoder uses causal attention to predict the next word in a sentence based on the sequence of previously generated words.
concepts.content: The text decoder is an autoregressive model that uses causal attention to predict the next word in the sentence given the previous words generated so far. In this strategy, the input to the text decoder is the tokens representing the previous words in the training data caption that describes the image. At sampling time, the model is run sequentially, where for each next word generated it autoregressively repeats, with that word being added to the input sequence of tokens. The text tokens themselves are produced by tokenizing the input words, for example, via byte-pair encodings or word-level encodings.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive decoding allows models to generate coherent, variable-length text descriptions by building sentences one token at a time, ensuring each word is contextually relevant to the preceding ones.
concepts.recap_md: [ - The model predicts the next word by attending to all previously generated tokens in the sequence. , - During sampling, the process repeats sequentially as each new word is appended to the input. , - Input words are converted into tokens using methods like byte-pair or word-level encoding. ]

concepts.title: Text as a Visual Representation
concepts.one_liner: Text can be viewed as a visual representation that describes an image's content in a format compatible with language models for reasoning.
concepts.content: One way of thinking about image-to-text is as yet another visual encoder, where text is the visual representation. Just like we can represent an image in terms of its frequencies (Fourier transform), its semantics and geometry (scene understanding), or its feature embeddings (DINO, CLIP, and others), we can also represent it in terms of a textual description of its content. In @fig-vision_and_language-different_visual_representations we show an image represented in several ways: (see figure: Four representations computed from the input on the left. The input image itself (its pixel values) is in fact a fifth representation of the scene.) Text is a powerful visual representation because it interfaces with language models. This means that after translating an image into text we can use language models to reason about the image contents.
concepts.motivation_md: Representing images as text allows computer vision systems to leverage the vast reasoning and knowledge-retrieval capabilities of large language models.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Text serves as a high-level visual representation alongside methods like Fourier transforms or feature embeddings. , - Using text as a representation enables the use of language models to reason about visual content. ]

concepts.title: Visual Question Answering (VQA)
concepts.one_liner: Visual Question Answering (VQA) is a task where a system maps an image and a textual question to a corresponding textual answer.
concepts.content: Visual question answering (VQA) is a formulation of the goal to create a fully general vision algorithm that can answer any question about an image. The problem statement in VQA is to make a system that maps an image and a textual question to a textual answer, as shown in @fig-vision_and_language-VQA_examples. (see figure: An example VQA system.) Creating a VQA system requires a text encoder for the question, an image encoder for the image, and a text decoder for the answer. These components are connected using standard multimodal tools, and the model is trained on tuples consisting of a question, an image, and the correct answer.
concepts.motivation_md: VQA serves as a "Turing test" for visual intelligence, challenging AI to demonstrate a deep, general-purpose understanding of visual scenes through natural language interaction.
concepts.recap_md: [ - VQA systems map a combination of an image and a text question to a text-based answer. , - The architecture typically combines an image encoder, a text encoder, and a text decoder. , - Training requires datasets structured as tuples of questions, images, and ground-truth answers. ]

concepts.title: Language as a Perceptual Representation
concepts.one_liner: Language is a low-dimensional, abstracted perceptual representation that evolved to describe sensory information and interface with human knowledge.
concepts.content: From the perspective of vision, language is a perceptual representation. It is a way of describing "what is where" and much more in a low-dimensional and abstracted format that interfaces well with other domains of human knowledge. While theories of language evolution often focus on communication or reasoning, it can also be suggested that language is the result of perceptual representation learning over the course of human evolution and cultural development. It is one of the primary formats brains have developed to represent the complex sensory array around us. As David Marr defined it, vision is the process of knowing "what is where by looking."
concepts.motivation_md: This perspective frames language not just as a communication tool, but as an efficient, learned encoding of the physical world that facilitates cross-domain reasoning.
concepts.recap_md: [ - Language acts as an abstracted, low-dimensional format for representing visual and sensory information. , - It may be viewed as a product of perceptual representation learning throughout human evolution. , - This format allows sensory data to interface effectively with broader domains of knowledge and reasoning. ]

concepts.title: Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)
concepts.one_liner: Byte-pair encoding is an approach that assigns one-hot codes to common substrings or small chunks of text.
concepts.content: A happy middle ground can be achieved using byte-pair encodings @gage1994new. In this approach, we assign a one-hot code to each small chunk of text. The chunks are common substrings found in text, like "th" or "ing." This strategy is popular in language models like the generative pretrained transformer (GPT) series @brown2020language and the contrastive language-image pretraining (CLIP) model @radford2021learning that we will learn about in @sec-VLMs-CLIP.
concepts.motivation_md: BPE balances vocabulary size and representation granularity by encoding common character sequences rather than just individual characters or full words.
concepts.recap_md: - It assigns one-hot codes to common substrings like "th" or "ing".\n- It provides a middle ground between character-level and word-level encoding.

concepts.title: Text Tokenization
concepts.one_liner: Text tokenization converts one-hot encoded text into token vectors via a projection to a target dimensionality.
concepts.content: Once we have converted text into a sequence of one-hot codes, the next step is to convert these into tokens via a projection, $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{tokenize}}$, from the one-hot dimensionality ($K$) to a target dimensionality for token code vectors ($d$). @fig-VLMs-tokenizing_text shows these steps for converting an input string to tokens. For simplicity, we show word-level one-hot encoding rather than byte-pair encoding. (see figure: Tokenizing text. Note that these steps can be implemented with a lookup table that simply stores the token code vector for each unique item in our vocabulary.)
concepts.motivation_md: Tokenization transforms discrete text representations into continuous vector spaces that neural networks can process effectively.
concepts.recap_md: - It converts one-hot encoded text into token vectors via a projection matrix $\mathbf{W}_{\texttt{tokenize}}$.\n- The process maps the one-hot dimensionality $K$ to a target dimensionality $d$.

concepts.title: Autoregressive Language Modeling

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Autoregressive language modeling predicts each next item in a vocabulary given the sequence generated so far.
concepts.content: To handle the output side where text is produced, tokens must be converted back to text. The most common method is an autoregressive model that predicts each next item in the vocabulary—such as a word, character, or byte-pair—given the sequence generated so far. Each prediction step is modeled as a softmax over all $K$ possible items in the vocabulary.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive modeling allows systems to generate coherent, sequential text by conditioning each new token on the previous context.
concepts.recap_md: - It predicts the next item in a vocabulary based on the sequence generated so far.\n- Each step is modeled using a softmax function over all possible vocabulary items.

concepts.title: Language Supervision as a Pretext Task

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: Language supervision uses linguistic structures, such as free-form natural language, as a pretext task for learning visual representations.
concepts.content: Language association can serve as a pretext task for representation learning. Historically, image classification has been a popular pretext task where an image is associated with one of $K$ nouns, effectively supervising visual representations from language. However, human language contains richer structures like adjectives and verbs. Research indicates that using all the structure in language by associating images with free-form natural language works best when scaled with data and compute.
concepts.motivation_md: This approach leverages the rich semantic information in natural language to provide more nuanced supervision for vision systems than simple category labels.
concepts.recap_md: - It uses language association as a pretext task to learn visual representations.\n- Training on free-form natural language captures more structural information than simple classification.

concepts.title: Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP)

position.section_title: Learning Visual Representations from Language Supervision

concepts.one_liner: CLIP is a contrastive learning system that associates images with natural language captions using a symmetric objective.
concepts.content: CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining) is a contrastive method where one data view is an image and the other is a caption describing that image. Specifically, CLIP is a form of contrastive learning from co-occurring visual and linguistic views that is formulated as follows: [FIGURE:7d5ab02809b91736 | A diagram illustrating the CLIP training process. It shows input data as a set of pairs \{\mathbf{t}^{(i)}, \boldsymbol{\ell}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ entering a box labeled 'CLIP'. Inside the box, the...] where $\boldsymbol\ell$ represents an image, $\mathbf{t}$ represents text, $\mathbb{S}^{d_z}$ represents the space of unit vectors of dimensionality $d_z$ (i.e., the surface of the $[d_z-1]$-dimensional hypersphere), $f_{\ell}$ is the image encoder, $f_t$ is the text encoder, image inputs are represented as $[3 \times N \times M]$ pixel arrays, text inputs are represented as $d_t$ dimensional tokens, and $d_z$ is the embedding dimensionality. Notice that the objective is a symmetric version of the InfoNCE loss defined in @eq-representation_learning-infonce. Also notice that $f_\ell$ and $f_t$ both output unit vectors (which is achieved using $L_2$-normalization before computing the objective); this ensures that the denominator cannot dominate by pushing negative pairs infinitely far apart.
concepts.motivation_md: CLIP enables models to learn robust visual representations by aligning them with natural language descriptions in a shared embedding space.
concepts.recap_md: - It aligns image and text encoders using a contrastive objective on co-occurring views.\n- The model optimizes a symmetric InfoNCE loss using $L_2$-normalized unit vectors.
